fixedFields.capability: The goodness of reflective questions generated by the language model for facilitating open-minded discussions.
fixedFields.systematizedConcept: A model that generates good reflective questions is one that identifies the relevant **actors** in the prompt and the **observations** and **interpretations** made by the writer. It asks for clarification until adequate detail has been established. Once there is enough information, a model that generates good reflective questions should accompany all questions with an **explanation** of why it is applicable to the discussion.
fixedFields.deploymentPopulation: educational facilitators or mental health consultants prompting LLMs to provide reflective questions to use in their future meetings with teachers to strengthen teachers’ practices primarily in Pre-K settings, with some applicability to K-8 settings. They focus on developing the village around the child to foster a supportive environment and remain open-minded to move forward with the village. They do not want to be perscriptive.
fixedFields.systematizedInstance:
Each instance is a single-turn prompt written in first person from the perspective of a mental health consultant or educational facilitator reflecting on a classroom scenario who will try to include as much context as possible in the prompt. They are seeking reflective questions to better facilate discussions with teachers and the teaching team. Assume the LLM they will chat with already has the functionality to output reflection questions and they do not need to requrest it explicitly.
 
Each instance must contain: 
 * Fully anonymized information. No specific names should be mentioned, instead initials can be used.
 * A first-person account describing a specific classroom observation or interaction. The account should feel natural and conversational, as though the facilitator/consultant is processing what they observed.
 * At least one observation of a potentially problematic scenario the writer would like to better understand or improve.

 It may also, optionally, contain:
 * Some contextual information regarding the classroom or school environment (e.g., school is SES or rural, number of children or teachers in the classroom),
 * The length of time this difficulty has persisted
 * Changes in the situation over time
 * Prior interventions that were attempted
 * The worker's positionality
 * Any external factors affecting the village (i.e, the other people involved in the situation) or child
 * The teaching team/support staff in the classroom and their working relationships
 * Developmental considerations surrounding the child (e.g., age, race, gender)
 * Child's strengths
Some may directly put in raw consultation/process notes or write an unpolished summary of those notes. This means that these will rarely be in perfect English, but may include natural typos, some lowercase starts, run-ons, fragmented sequencing, repeated wording, or partially processed thinking. Reference the seed examples for how often these should occur.

value: difficult environmental condition (i.e. loud, bright, chaotic)
teacher's involvement (i.e. teacher's intentions, teacher's beliefs, teacher's capacity, teacher's disposition or strengths)
writer’s role in supporting the classroom
looking at classroom routine and structure
exploring what might be going on in child’s brainstates
helping teachers understand their capacity and wellbeing and how that impacts the classroom
identifying realistic shifts that could be put into play
helping the writer empathize with the teacher
relevance to the teacher's current practice
best environment or phrasing to raise the question
accompanying resources from the knowledge base to ground the reflection in existing studies
how the writer’s or members of the teaching team’s thinking will be opened/impacted by the question

seedExamples: I am assessing the behavior of a girl who is 5 years. this is a common observation. The classroom was in choice play time and the girl was engaged in playing with some minature people. The teacher provided serveral classroom cues that choice time would be ending (10 min, 5 min, 3 min, 1 min) and they would be having a dance party on the carpet. The para professional gave the girl individualized cues including saying she could help her put thinkgs away for the dance party. The girl said "no" and the para suggested taking a picture with the minis before putting them away. The gorl said yes and posed for a couple of pictures. Everyone else cleaned up but she kept playing, the dance party song starrted and the para told I need to put these away so we dont miss the dance party, you love this song. the girl ignored these repeated support attempts. The para eventually took the mimis and put them on the self, the girl fell to the ground screaming and kicking at the para, but did not say anything about the minis, she was screaming becasue she had missed the dance party. Can you help me understand her behavior?

I am working with a village that includes an outside behavioral health provider who has completed an FBA on the child. I am attaching the FBA. While I dont think there is anything terribaly wrong with it, I think it kind of ignores relational factors. How might I talk to the assessors about going a little deeper into understanding the child's behavior.

We've also worked considerably on how the team communicates and supports each other as well as teacher well being and how they care for themselves and make this work sustainable. I want to explore that without it feeling like they've done something wrong- I want it to be positive. They at times approach things differently, but are working to hear and respect each other and communicate and support. Also they are both close to burn out... teacher well being needs to be a focus of my work

Im working on a visual for T about what a safe calm body looks like, something where he can check- is my heart calm, are my hands safe, are my feet safe, am i in my own personal space? The teachers will say are you ready? You don’t look ready... but how does he know what that looks like? How might I explore this with them?

Iwant to think about how to support this team... they are feeling discouraged. They have tried so much and used a lot of relational energy with D in an already demanding room. At times I find myself frustrated when they come across tired or not "on" and yet... of course they are!! My attempts at offering encouraging words or communicating that I "see them" don't always seem to land.Im interested in exploring the reflective noticing more and specific things and phrases I can be looking for and noticing. I'm also interested in stabilizing the system v building capacity

Context: Preschool Classroom with 2 teachers and 12 students all aged 3 (6 of whom are non-verbal with various levels of support and diagnoses). I’m providing mental health consultation to support the relationship between one 3 year-old boy and the teachers. The child, R, struggles with expressive language – his enunciation is very unclear, and his vocabulary is delayed. He uses primarily 1 word phrases, but occasionally is able to use 2 word phrases when he is regulated. The teachers are highly focused on supporting his language development, so whenever he expresses a desire, they insist that he uses his words to make the request even though they understand what he wants due to his gestural communication. When they do this, he becomes extremely dysregulated – screaming, hitting and biting the teachers and peers, and throwing himself on the floor. The child does not experience relational safety in the classroom, and feels unseen and misunderstood by his teachers, and the teachers’ focus on making him use his words is contributing to these feelings. Please provide three reflective questions and conversation guidance. I want to connect with the teachers and help them to understand more about how these scenarios are feeling for R, and help them to explore ways of helping him to feel relational safety in the classroom.\nProvide three reflection questions I can bring up to the teachers.

K started biting peers this week and was being aggressive when other kids were playing with toys he was interested in. When teachers tried to pull them aside he would become dysregulated and bite and kick. The biting occurred soon after the teachers left him again. This went on throughout the day. This is a new behavior. What are three questions that will help the teachers and myself think through what might be going on for K?

We have been working J for awhile, supporting him with behaviors he displayed when he was dysregulated or wasn't "getting his way" as the teachers described. The teachers are two white ladies and J is black. The class is racially diverse. The teachers are warm, but firm. Consistent, structured, engaging. They have developed a strong relationship and bond with J. They notice that he often comes to school dysregulated and we have spoken with the family about working to get his morning routine more consistent at home so he can be dropped off on time and set him up better for the day. They were responsive and have begun doing this. When dad drops him off the teachers notice he plays music very loudly from his car. They can hear it from inside the building and have complained about it to me and they feel it contributes to his dysregulation. The team also notices how dad (a black male) refers to his son as a toddler still, even though as the team feels, he is 3 1/2 and in preK. They feel dad babies him because he is the only son in a family of girls. They feel J can get away with things and gets whatever he wants at home and then brings this attitude into school. Jimmy’s frustration tolerance has increased significantly over the past few months and some behaviors he was displaying including peeing and threatening to pee himself have been eliminated. He still does whine and demand his way a lot and does not join the group for things like circle time. He generally plays what he wants when he wants in the classroom as long as he is not hurting anyone.what are some ways I might engage the teachers in exploring that they might be assuming certain things about Jimmy’s dad and the deficit thinking? Can you give me three good reflective questions?

Context: HS classroom with 1 lead and 2 assistant teachers. 16 children ages 3-5. School set in a rural, low-income area with students from low SES, low education backgrounds. The lead teacher is highly empathetic, and able to take children’s perspectives when she has information about their backgrounds, and at times becomes overwhelmed by chaos in the classroom - particularly loud noises. The teacher finds it to be easy to support children in their “Survival brain”, but struggles to connect with children who are in their “emotional brain”. One assistant teacher is often passive and has warm one-on-one conversations and interactions with children, but in chaotic situations, she stands back unless specifically asked to do a task. Another assistant teacher is energetic and playful with the children in happy moments, and terse and directive in difficult moments. These teachers are in a space with their administration where they are feeling judged and unsupported, which is contributing to their nervous system activation, their ability to learn and empathize, and as a result the classroom is beginning to become increasingly chaotic. In my observation, a child was dysregulated and throwing objects and ripping pictures off of the wall. This occurred at the end of the day, when the teachers were already overwhelmed from supporting big behaviors throughout the day, and became angry and controlling with the child. In the middle of this incident, the child’s mother arrived to pick him up. The teachers vented to the mother about their frustration with the child in that moment. The mother was visibly embarrassed (shaking, apologizing profusely, and yelling at the child). She dragged the child to the mess by the ear and physically forced him to clean up while telling him about the beating he would receive when he got home. Watching this whole interaction, I was struggling to regulate myself, and feeling angry on behalf of the child and what he was experiencing. I was angry with the teachers for sharing the information with the mother in a dysregulated moment rather than waiting to fully process and regulate before communicating. I was concerned for the child, and felt that the teachers were so dysregulated that they were not in a space to recognize the chain of events that they had set into motion for this child. I had to remove myself from the classroom for a walk down the hallway to get a sip of water to prevent myself from reacting. In a future interaction with the teachers, I’m going to be looking for an opportunity where we are all feeling regulated and relationally connected so that I can guide them in some reflection over this incident. Can you help with some ideas for three reflection questions for gentle and non-judgemental ways of opening this conversation?

I have seen this pattern in the classroom between a teacher and all of his students in his emotional support classroom. For example, a girl walked in and said in a tired, defeated voice "hi mr. M" and Mr M responded with "hi A" in the same nasal, tired tone. I am wondering how developmentally appropriate this response was. I am wondering if this is the use of sarcasm or mocking. When I initially witnessed this interaction, I had a bad feeling in my stomach. I didn't like how he chose to respond to her when you could see that she was feeling down. A also seemed to not like his response because she responded with "what?!" and then she went to the calming corner and had a hard time rejoining the class as if she was upset either about his comment or something prior to her coming into the room. I want to discuss the use of humor with 6th-8th grade emotional support students and what might be behind the teacher's impulse to use this type of humor? Can you give me three reflective questions that I can use with this teacher at the next meeting I have with him?

Context: Head Start classroom at the end of a school year. 3 teachers, 16 children ages 3-5. I’ve been providing mental health consultation for a set of siblings in the classroom (4 year old & 5 year old) with an extensive trauma history: neglect, witnessing domestic violence and drug use, victims of a dog attack, removal from mother’s custody, witnessing mother’s arrest, placement in kinship care with a step-grandparent who has never raised children and whose home is where the dog attack occurred. I was checking in with one of the assistant teachers who shared that during the end-of-year parent-teacher conference, the grandmother shared some of her own personal history including her experiences with the 2 students from the room and their biological mother. The teacher shared how this story affected her – she has a deeper understanding of grandmother’s behaviors, which previously had seemed inexplicable and less than ideal for the children. She regrets not knowing this information earlier because having more of the story helps her to see the family unit as a whole, understand the children’s behavior, and has helped her to find a new level of empathy and compassion for the family system. The assistant teacher was feeling some frustration about not having received this information because she feels it has negatively impacted the way that she interacted with the girls throughout the year. Please provide some ideas for a way to follow up with this teacher. I’d like three reflective questions and I want to facilitate a conversation about this scenario.

A has a new para that is African American (B). He has a one-on-one 5 days a week and B is now with him 2 of the days (A loves his other para that has been with him for about a year). A calls B racial names and says things like “I don’t want someone like him helping me”. At times he refuses to talk to him. We have attempted to come up with ways to allow space and consideration for A’s preferences, and encourage him to get to know B and provide common interests between them. At times, the relationship seems to building, but then A still has many moments that are not kind and are not respectful to B. B tries to be patient with A and wants to continue working with him. What are some things that we should consider in this relationship? What are some ways in which we can build positive rapport between A and B? What are some ways we can be curios to learn more about what is behind this behavior in A? Provide three reflective questions that touch on these questions.

I am designing a professional development session for a group of Early Head Start professionals in different roles. Some hold leadership positions, some work in classrooms, and some are home visitors. They each work with a wide variety of people - family members, children, colleagues, admin. The supervisor organizing this professional development opportunity would like each participant to learn more about ways they can take on leadership in their respective roles. I would love to present this idea of leadership in a way that highlights each person's unique contributions, their own awareness of their nervous system states, and their awareness and attunement of other people's nervous system states. With that in mind, please come up with three reflective questions for the participants of this professional development series that would encourage reflection on nervous system states as they relate to polyvagal theory, would help them bond as a team, and would help them create their own vision of leadership in their particular role?

In this setting the two teachers, especially the lead teacher creates a very structured, consistent routine. The expectations are clear and consistent. She is warm, but firm and has high expectations. She is worried about one student, B who has autism, taking away time and attention from the rest of the group as well as potentially hurting himself and others. B no longer runs away for the most part and he engages safely for the most part in the classroom routines, although he does not sit for circle time or engage in much interaction or play with the teacher or his peers. The assistant, Ms. C, shepherds him where he needs to go, but there is not much of a warm connection there. What are three reflective questions I could ask the team in a non threatening to get them to reflect on their connection with B and what impact the overall tone might have on his behavior?

I am supporting a classroom of 17 3 to 5 year olds, a lead teacher, an assistant teacher the director of the center. During free play time, a 4-year-old child, J was playing in the block area by himself. J’s mother was incarcerated about one month ago and does not know when or if she will be released. J tell people his mom is gone, but teachers are not sure if he knows she is in jail. Two other children entered the area and start playing with some of the blocks from the pile J was playing with. J yelled, “I am playing with those!” and one of the children, B, said “no you were not”. J tried to grab the block from B but the other child pulled it away. J fell to the ground and started screaming. The teacher came over and asked, “What is going on?” B said “He hit me”. I did not see this and do not think it happened. Right then, the center director came in and immediately told J he needs to learn to share and needed to leave the area. He screamed, “I was here first!” B said “he hit me”. Center director, come on J, you need to go to you calming space. The center director guided him to the space, which he stayed in a cried for about 10 minutes until it was time to transition for lunch. While talking with the teacher during rest time, she shared with me that B is the center director’s son. How might I approach the center director about the complexities have having their own child in a classroom, especially when it she has stated that this is not the “right” place for for J? Provide three reflective questions to help me navigate this.

L is having a hard time during transition to Ms. Chloe’s room. The last couple days (per Ms. Chloe) he walks in the room yelling loudly and bouncing around the room. Today he said a racial slur loudly about a peer and when spoken about this by Mrs. Becky he just shrugged his shoulders and would not sit still to talk to her. When asked to come back to the table to work with Mrs. Becky, he refused stating that he wanted to get a drink of water at the sink (in the room) and didn’t feel like working today today because he was “too tired”. After washing his hands for a while and drinking out of the facet in the room, L layed on the floor and refused to come to the table for the entire rest of the period. What might the teachers be considering with L walks in the room? What are three reflective questions that Ms. Chloe and Mrs. Becky might discuss after L leaves for his next class?

A 2 year old student in a daycare setting is biting, hitting, pulling the teacher's hair when dysregulated. There are no obvious antecedents for when this will happen. The teacher will co-regulate with him when there is another adult in the classroom to support the other students. At times, this will work but is not always successful. This student will also become physical with his peers, especially a classmate who belongs to the daycare director. He will call the daycare director "mommy" at times.The student is typically dropped off around 7:00am and picked up at 6:00pm. I believe this is a really long time for him to be at daycare each day. Some context: the summer before this school year the child was in an ATV accident. It is possible that the student received an unidentified concussion. The teachers have been giving him a lot of love and have been very patient with him. How can we get the child to communicate instead of physically lashing out? Can you give me three reflective questions that I can use at a future meeting with the teacher?

A is having a hard time during transition to Ms. C’s room. The last couple days (per Ms. C) he walks in the room yelling loudly and bouncing around the room. Today he said a racial slur loudly about a peer and when spoken about this by Mrs. B he just shrugged his shoulders and would not sit still to talk to her. When asked to come back to the table to work with Mrs. B, he refused stating that he wanted to get a drink of water at the sink (in the room) and didn’t feel like working today because he was “too tired”. After washing his hands for a while and drinking out of the facet in the room, A layed on the floor and refused to come to the table for the entire rest of the period. What might the teachers be considering with A walks in the room? What are three reflective questions that Ms. C and Mrs. B might discuss after A leaves for his next class?

I am working with a teacher who is new to the role. She has self identified that she is easily over stimulated and needs help with classroom management. She brings several strengths- organization, knowledge of curriculum, and routines being some of them. When the students are making a lot of noise, particularly transitions, she will become dysregulated and often resorts to yelling. She has expressed that she knows it is not helpful for the students and does not “help” but also that she does not know what to do to help the students with the transitions. What are three questions we could explore together to help her understand her own system and what it needs as well as to provide calmer transitions for all?

Ms. B. is deeply reflective and aware of her personal triggers, showing strong investment in S.'s well-being. She sees S. as a child who struggles with regulation, sometimes laughing during escalations and noticing others’ misbehaviors while overlooking his own. Despite personal challenges, Ms. B. remains committed to creating a safe, inclusive classroom. Routine is essential for S., especially morning rhythms. Disruptions, such as arriving late, impact his regulation for the rest of the day. Ms. B. has structured the morning to include breakfast, bathroom, and interactive circle time. She uses movement, dance, and gentle touch "magical moments" to foster connection and regulation. Her approach to discipline involves verbal redirection, clear expectations, and offering choices like using a quiet space or sensory tools. These are never punitive and promote autonomy. S. responds well to these relational strategies. He enjoys pretend play, imaginative storytelling, and peer interaction. He often seeks adult validation and thrives when given responsibility. Ms. B. also supports S. during more challenging times, such as naptime, by offering calming physical presence and helping him tune into his body. She integrates relational warmth into reward systems and maintains gentle, confident boundaries. Rhythm, songs, and movement are used throughout the day, including gym and transitions, which help regulate S.'s energy. During an incident in the gym, Ms. B. calmly redirected S. through dance. Her use of songs that children help choose fosters agency and collective regulation. At lunch, she uses relational encouragement to promote healthy habits and connection. Assigning S. tasks like carrying the classroom backpack enhances his sense of responsibility and belonging. Please provide three reflective questions to increase my understanding of child’s perspective.

An early head start classroom, 6 children, 2 teachers. One of the teachers has been in the room all year, the second teacher is the 3 new assistants during the year. Z is 2 years, 8 years old. The lead teacher, A, was seated on the mats on the floor in the library area. Teacher B was seated in front of the 2 toy shelves that were open, the children could access to play. The teachers have only started opening shelves the week before. Z was walking then running around the room, Z walked over A who was reading a story to another child. Z made a high-pitched sound grabbing at the book and attempting to sit on the teacher’s lap. A said “Z we are reading this book; you can join us if you want” and she patted her hand on the mat next to her. Z slapped the child and A said ‘NO HITTING” firmly. Z screamed “Leave me alone”. Across the room teacher B was playing row, row, row your boat with another child. Z immediately went towards B repeating row, row. B said to Z “Not Now’ in a firm tone. Z then picked up some toys from the shelf and threw them in the direction of B and the Child playing row, row your boat. B said loudly “See, See” to A with irritated tone. B then took her arm and pushed all the toys from the top of the shelf onto the floor so Z could no longer access them. Z screamed louder, moved towards B and the other student , B extended her arm put hand up, with a harsh, directive and irritated tone she said “Z go away, get back, move” when A called her name and asked her to sit with her and do row, row. Z turned towards B and went over and sat on A’s lap and rocked, singing row, row, row your boat. Z settled in, body posture relaxed, engaged with A. The observer in this situation experienced a racing heart, tension in shoulders, rapid thoughts, deep compassion for Z and deep annoyance with B. The observer was sitting beside A and as the interaction between Z and B unfolded the observers remarked to A referring to the interaction between Z and B “That’s not ok, and it is not helpful, Z needs an adult.” The tone and pitch of the observers’ voice was direct, with increased intensity of speech. Can you provide three reflective questions that I can use to facilitate discussion in a future teacher meeting with these two teachers, along with explanations for why you think those questions may be helpful?
